description: A fundamental hip throw where you load your opponent onto your hip and rotate them to the ground.
A major outer reaping throw. You reap your opponent's leg from the outside while breaking their balance backward.
A shoulder throw where you load your opponent onto your back and throw them forward over your shoulder.
Scarf hold. A fundamental pinning technique where you control your opponent by holding their head and arm while seated beside them.
Side four-quarter hold. You control your opponent from the side, securing both their hips and head.
Cross armlock. You hyperextend your opponent's elbow joint by placing their arm across your hips while lying perpendicular to them.
A one-arm shoulder throw. You control your opponent's sleeve and slide your other arm under their armpit before dropping under them and throwing them over your back.
A major inner reaping throw. You reap your opponent's leg from the inside while driving them backward off balance.
An advancing foot sweep. You sweep your opponent's foot the instant they shift their weight onto it, timing the sweep with their own step.
A shoulder pin. You trap your opponent's head and one arm against your shoulder while lying perpendicular across their upper body.
Upper four-quarter hold. You control your opponent from above their head, pinning both arms and driving your weight down onto their chest.
Vertical four-quarter hold. You straddle your opponent's torso, pinning them chest-to-chest facing the same direction.
A body drop. You block your opponent's leg with your own while pulling and rotating them forward over the obstruction.
A hip wheel. You wrap your arm around your opponent's neck and pivot them over your hip like a turning wheel.
A sweeping hip throw. You load your opponent onto your hip and sweep their leg out from under them as you rotate.
A minor inner reaping throw. You hook your opponent's heel from the inside with a small reaping motion to drop them backward.
A minor outer reaping throw. You reap your opponent's heel from the outside just as they step, dropping them straight back.
A sliding foot sweep. You sweep both of your opponent's feet together as they shift sideways, timing the sweep with their step.
A knee wheel. You block your opponent's knee with your foot and pivot them over the block as you pull them off balance.
A modified scarf hold. A variation of Kesa-gatame where you switch your underneath arm to trap around your opponent's far arm instead of controlling their head.
A modified upper four-quarter hold. A variation of Kami-shiho-gatame where you reach under one of your opponent's arms for a tighter, lower control.
A reverse scarf hold. You pin your opponent facing away from their legs, the mirror image of the standard Kesa-gatame position.
A rear naked strangle. Attacking from behind, you wrap an arm around your opponent's neck and squeeze both carotid arteries without gripping the jacket.
An entangled armlock. You bend your opponent's elbow to a right angle and rotate their shoulder joint by weaving your arm through theirs.
A shoulder drop. Similar to Seoi-nage, but instead of throwing your opponent over your shoulder, you drop your knee and pull them down in front of you.
A lift-pull hip throw. You lift your opponent up and forward with both hands before dropping your hips under them and rotating them over.
A lifting hip throw. You reach around your opponent's waist with your free arm and lift them onto your hip before rotating them over.
A spring hip throw. You load your opponent onto your hip and spring your leg up into their thigh to launch them over.
A minor outer hook. You hook your leg around the outside of your opponent's leg and drive them backward without lifting your foot off the mat.
A leg wheel. You block your opponent's leg with your straightened leg and pivot them over it, similar to Hiza-guruma but higher on the leg.
A major wheel throw. You block your opponent's leg with your own straightened leg while pulling them up and over it in a large circular motion.
A major outer drop. Similar to O-soto-gari but without the reaping leg contact — you drop your opponent backward using upper-body control alone.
A major outer wheel. Like O-soto-gari, but you block both of your opponent's legs with your own leg for a wider, more controlling sweep.
A circle throw. You drop onto your back, plant a foot in your opponent's abdomen, and pull them up and over you in a circular arc.
A valley drop. You step behind your opponent's leg to block it, then drop your own weight backward to fall them over the obstruction.
A supporting foot-lift throw. You block your opponent's ankle with your foot while lifting and pulling them forward over the block.
A reverse hold. You pin your opponent from above while facing their feet, controlling them chest-to-chest in the opposite orientation from Kami-shiho-gatame.
A normal cross strangle. Both palms face inward as you cross your arms and grip your opponent's collar, squeezing both sides of their neck evenly.
A half cross strangle. One palm faces in and one faces out as you cross your arms and grip the collar, applying more pressure on one side of the neck.
A reverse cross strangle. Both palms face outward as you cross your arms and grip your opponent's collar, the mirror version of Nami-juji-jime.
An arm-crush armlock. You trap your opponent's straightened arm against your own arm or shoulder and lever it to hyperextend the elbow.
An arm-crush armlock. You clamp your opponent's arm under your armpit, trapping their wrist against your body while extending their elbow.
A shoulder wheel. You duck low, take your opponent onto your shoulders like a fireman's carry, and rotate them off to the side.
A sleeve lift-pull hip throw. Gripping both sleeves, you lift your opponent up and forward before rotating them over your hip.
An inner-thigh counter-throw. As your opponent attempts Uchi-mata, you shift your hips out of range and pull them past you off balance.
A floating hip throw. You wrap your arm around your opponent's waist and rotate them across the front of your hip without much lift.
A rear hip throw, typically used as a counter. You wrap your arms around your opponent's waist from the front and lift them backward over your hip.
A swallow counter throw. As your opponent attempts a foot sweep, you lift your leg out of the way and sweep their supporting leg instead.
An inner-thigh throw. You sweep your leg up between your opponent's legs against their inner thigh while pulling them forward and around.
An outer wrap-around throw. You wrap your arm around your opponent's arm and sacrifice your own balance, rolling them over as you fall to the outside.
A minor inner wrap-around throw. Combining Ko-uchi-gari's reap with a wrapping arm, you roll your opponent over as you drop to the mat.
A corner throw. You drop straight back onto the mat, hooking a leg behind your opponent's knee and pulling them over you as you fall.
A side drop. You drop your body sideways to the mat while pulling your opponent's upper body down, sweeping their legs out from under them.
A side wheel, typically used as a counter to a hip throw. You drop sideways to the mat while pulling your opponent over and past you.
A floating pin. A lighter, more mobile hold where you control your opponent's arm and body with your weight balanced above rather than fully settled.
A sliding collar strangle. Attacking from behind, you use one hand to pull the collar across the throat while the other hand slides in to reinforce the choke.
A single-wing strangle. You pin one of your opponent's arms behind their back while choking with the collar, removing their ability to defend.
The full name for the technique you already know as Juji-gatame — the cross armlock, extending your opponent's elbow across your hips while lying perpendicular to them.
An arm-crush armlock. You trap your opponent's arm against your knee, using your leg rather than your torso as the lever to extend their elbow.
A mountain-storm throw. A hybrid of a hand throw and a leg block — you pull your opponent forward while sweeping their leg out with your own.
A floating drop. With no leg contact at all, you break your opponent's balance forward and drop them purely through timing and rotation of your arms.
A corner drop. You break your opponent's balance toward their back corner and drop them straight down with no significant leg or hip contact.
A switching hip throw, used as a counter. As your opponent lifts you onto their hip, you switch your hips underneath theirs and reverse the throw.
A belt-grab counter throw. You grip your opponent's belt directly and lift them up and over, typically countering a failed hip or shoulder throw attempt.
A lift-pull sweeping ankle throw. You sweep your opponent's leg while lifting and pulling with your arms, similar to Sasae but with a sweeping rather than blocking leg action.
A pulling-in counter throw. You drop to the mat while pulling your opponent's sleeve and lapel down and around, rolling them over your body.
A rear throw. You wrap your arms around your opponent's torso from the front, arch backward, and throw them over your head to the mat behind you.
A floating sacrifice throw. You drop to the side while pulling your opponent forward and off balance, sweeping their supporting leg away.
A rice-bale counter throw. As your opponent attacks with a bent-over technique, you wrap around their torso and roll them backward over your body.
A sweeping wrap-around throw. You combine a sweeping leg action with wrapping your arm around your opponent's arm and sacrificing your balance to roll them over.
A major outer wrap-around throw. Combining O-soto-gari's reaping action with a wrapping arm, you sacrifice your own balance to roll your opponent over as you fall.
A thrusting strangle. You drive one hand deep across your opponent's collar while the other hand pulls the same lapel down, crossing your arms at the wrists.
A triangle strangle. You lock your legs around your opponent's neck and one arm in a figure-four, using leg pressure to cut off blood flow.
A sleeve wheel strangle. You choke with one hand across the collar while your other hand controls your opponent's sleeve to prevent them from defending.
An arm-crush armlock. From a triangle leg position, you trap your opponent's arm between your legs and extend their elbow while your legs control their neck and shoulder.
A side sacrifice throw. You drop to the mat on your side while pulling your opponent forward and off balance, throwing them past you.
An embracing sacrifice throw. You wrap both arms around your opponent's upper body and drop to your side, pulling them over you as you fall.
A side hook. You hook your leg around your opponent's leg from the side while sacrificing your own balance, dropping them sideways to the mat.
An inner wrap-around throw. You trap your opponent's arm against your body and rotate forward, sacrificing your balance to roll them over your shoulder.
A wrap-around version of Uchi-mata. You combine the inner-thigh sweep with wrapping your opponent's arm, sacrificing your balance to roll them over.
A wrap-around version of Hane-goshi. You combine the springing hip action with wrapping your opponent's arm, sacrificing your balance to roll them over.
A minor inner counter throw. As your opponent attempts Ko-uchi-gari against you, you lift your leg clear and reverse the throw back onto them.
A major outer counter throw. As your opponent attempts O-soto-gari, you block their reaping leg and throw them backward before they complete it.
A major inner counter throw. As your opponent attempts O-uchi-gari, you block their reaping leg and reverse the throw back onto them.
A sweeping hip counter throw. As your opponent loads you onto their hip for Harai-goshi, you block their sweeping leg and throw them instead.
A spring hip counter throw. As your opponent loads you onto their hip for Hane-goshi, you block their springing leg and reverse the throw back onto them.
An inner-thigh counter throw. As your opponent attempts Uchi-mata, you block their sweeping leg and throw them backward before they complete it.
A one-hand strangle. Using only one hand deep across the collar, you apply choking pressure while your other arm controls your opponent's body.
A two-hand strangle. Both hands grip deep into the collar from the front, crossing at the wrists to compress both sides of the neck evenly.
An arm-crush armlock. You trap your opponent's arm against your stomach, using your torso as the lever to extend their elbow.
An arm-crush armlock. You trap your opponent's arm between your legs, using leg pressure rather than your arms to extend their elbow.
An arm-crush armlock. You pin your opponent's wrist and hand directly, using your hands alone to lever and extend their elbow joint.
A leg entanglement throw. You hook your leg around your opponent's leg from behind and fall backward, taking them down with you.
A scissor throw. You jump and clamp both legs around your opponent's leg and torso, scissoring them down to the mat.
A heel-trip counter throw. You grab your opponent's heel directly with your hand and lift it as they step forward, tipping them backward.
A single-leg takedown. You grab behind your opponent's knee with one hand while pushing their upper body over with the other.
A double-leg takedown. You drop low and grab behind both of your opponent's knees with both hands, driving them backward to the mat.
A belt-drop throw. You grip your opponent's belt directly with one hand and lift them up and over.
A scooping throw. You duck low and scoop both of your opponent's legs out from under them with your arms.
A leg entanglement lock. You trap your opponent's leg and hyperextend their knee or ankle joint by wrapping and controlling the limb.
A body scissor choke. You wrap your legs around your opponent's torso and squeeze to compress their ribs and diaphragm.
